steering_ledger.verbatim: Also, it may be possible that what optimized perfomance on half instances generalizes to full instances, so you could at least periodically experiment on two CPU kernels in parallel
steering_ledger.effect: Proposes a THIRD concurrency axis beyond the CPU/GPU lane split of seq 11: partition the CPU into two half-machine instances and screen TWO CPU kernel candidates in parallel, on the hypothesis that half-instance improvements generalize to full-instance. Supporting prior from our own measurements: NPS4 48t reaches 46.6 t/s against 96t-single at 49.1, i.e. the half-machine operating point is close enough that ranking may well be preserved. TWO CONSTRAINTS THAT MUST BE DESIGNED IN, NOT ASSUMED: (a) a half-machine result may SCREEN but may never GATE a full-machine claim — that is the standing gate-scope-must-match-measured-subset rule, and our canonical baseline protocol is explicitly full-machine (taskset 0-95, -t 96); (b) two concurrent CPU instances contend invisibly unless placement is forced, because mmap SHARES NUMA placement across instances — only --no-mmap plus explicit membind gives node-local isolation. WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT SHAPE: it makes half->full a MEASURED per-change-class transfer ratio rather than an assumption, which is exactly the mechanism the intake-1075 dive recommends importing (their measured classes: kernel/occupancy/precision 1.0-1.94x, sync/launch-pipeline ~0.5x, RL-routing ~0). Bandwidth-bound changes should transfer poorly (bandwidth-per-core differs between half and full) while instruction-level changes should transfer well — which is itself the testable prediction. Net effect on cadence: up to 3 concurrent screening lanes (GPU + 2x half-CPU), which materially narrows the parallelism gap against the Cholesky campaign's elastic containers.

steering_ledger.verbatim: mayeb even quarter instances or more!
steering_ledger.effect: Extends seq 12 from a half/full binary to PARTITION DEPTH AS A TUNABLE. NPS4 gives four natural NUMA domains (24 physical cores each), so quarter instances are the topology's own partition and deeper splits are measurable. Existing support in our record: we have measured deep CPU partitioning before (4x48t -> 32x6t, +44-58% on concurrent throughput) and we already run a quarter-fleet mode in the serving lineup, so the partitioning machinery is not new work. THE DESIGN INSIGHT: partition depth is a knob and screening validity is a SURFACE, not a constant — transfer fidelity should degrade as instances shrink, because a quarter instance has roughly a quarter of the memory bandwidth while CPU decode is bandwidth-bound, so the operating point diverges further from the full-machine baseline the deeper you partition. The right deliverable is therefore a 2D map: per CHANGE CLASS x PARTITION DEPTH, does candidate RANKING survive? Then screen at the shallowest depth that preserves ranking for the class being tested. Mechanistic prediction to pre-register: bandwidth-bound changes lose rank fidelity fast with depth; instruction-level/compute-bound changes hold. VALIDATION METHOD: run one fixed candidate set at full / half / quarter and measure rank correlation against the full-machine ordering — that is a screening-tier calibration, needs no new candidates, and is exactly the proxy->ground-truth transfer measurement the intake-1075 dive recommends importing. Cadence consequence: up to 5 concurrent screening lanes (1 GPU + 4 quarter-CPU), which closes most of the parallelism gap I had been treating as fixed against the Cholesky campaign's elastic containers.

steering_ledger.verbatim: beyond half instances the aggregate throughput takes a hit, but for the purposes of kernel development, the faster kernel experiment churn on short benchmark tasks is more important than maximizing absolute taskthroughput (like the orchestrator cares for)
steering_ledger.plan_ref: autokernel-research-loop.md §21 correction 3 (objective is experiment churn; only rank inversion costs)
steering_ledger.effect: THE CONCEPTUAL REFRAME OF THE SESSION, and it inverts the standing analysis. AutoKernel and the orchestrator have DIFFERENT OBJECTIVE FUNCTIONS over the same hardware. The orchestrator maximizes absolute task throughput, which is what our canonical CPU protocol is built for (full machine, taskset 0-95, -t 96) and why deep partitioning has always been scored as a throughput LOSS. Kernel development maximizes EXPERIMENT CHURN over short benchmark tasks, where aggregate tokens/sec is close to irrelevant: four quarter-instances completing four short benchmarks concurrently beat one full instance completing one, even though total throughput is lower. So the aggregate-throughput hit beyond half instances is NOT A COST for this workload — it is spending a resource the loop does not value to buy the one it does. CONSEQUENCE FOR PARTITION DEPTH: choose depth to maximize (experiments per hour x rank fidelity), NOT to maximize throughput. Throughput loss is acceptable at any depth; RANK INVERSION is the only real failure, so rank correlation against the full-machine ordering is the single binding constraint on how deep we may go. This also supplies the missing piece for the intake-1075 'hypothesis quality x useful experiments per unit time' thesis: that framing has no teeth without a lever on the second factor, and partition depth IS that lever on the CPU side. It further connects to objective-task-rate-goodput.md, which flipped live dominance to task_rate_4d_v1 on 2026-08-04 on exactly the argument that the throughput-shaped metric was the wrong objective for the real goal — the same category error, one level up.

steering_ledger.verbatim: also... if we profile specific bottlenecks, we could parallelize JUST that specific bottleneck operation in an attempt to experiment more quickly on how it can be optimized
steering_ledger.effect: COMPLETES the churn-not-throughput argument (seq 12-14) by identifying the unit of work that actually parallelizes. Whole-model benchmarks parallelize badly: large resident footprint, model load time, minutes per run, and system-level memory-bandwidth coupling between concurrent instances. A SINGLE OP microbenchmark parallelizes well: small tensors, no model load, milliseconds per run, and trivially pinnable to one NUMA domain. So the highest-churn screening tier is op-level, not model-level, and the concurrency ceiling there is much higher than the 4-5 lanes of seq 13. THE INFRASTRUCTURE ALREADY EXISTS: test-backend-ops IS an op-level harness and the intake-1085 dive established it as our standing T0 gate; rocprofv2 (side-loaded, version-matched, 465 counters enumerated on our own card) supplies the bottleneck identification; and autokernel-research-loop.md §9.4's wall-share rule (operator wall share x operator gain) is exactly the selector for WHICH op deserves the campaign. So the pipeline is profile -> select by wall share -> fan out many concurrent op-level experiments on the selected op -> promote survivors to graph level. THE BINDING CAVEAT, and it is measured rather than hypothetical: op-in-isolation is not op-in-graph. The intake-1087 (KForge) dive found per-kernel wins of 1.06-1.43x delivering +2.12% end-to-end against TensorRT-LLM, with the mechanism named (register/shared-memory pressure shifts and autotuner perturbation of neighbouring kernels). So op-level is a SCREEN whose transfer ratio to graph level must be MEASURED per change class, which is the same per-change-class transfer machinery the intake-1075 dive recommends importing (their measured classes: kernel/occupancy/precision 1.0-1.94x, sync/launch-pipeline ~0.5x, RL-routing ~0). One mechanism, three uses: half->full partition transfer, op->graph transfer, and T1->T3 tier transfer are all the same field on the evaluation event.

steering_ledger.verbatim: after experimenting on parallel lanes we'd still verify performance gains on a full instance as we always do when benchmarking. My point is that you coudl iterate faster using multiple instances and anly verify improvements on the single instance
steering_ledger.plan_ref: AK-LN-5 + §21 lane rule "lanes screen, the full instance verifies"
steering_ledger.effect: RE-CALIBRATES a risk the orchestrator overstated. Parallel/partitioned lanes are for ITERATION AND SCREENING ONLY; every claimed improvement is still verified on a full single instance under the canonical protocol, exactly as today. CONSEQUENCE: cross-lane interference (thermal, power, clock, memory-bandwidth coupling) cannot corrupt a CLAIM, because no claim is ever made from a lane. Its only cost is SEARCH EFFICIENCY — a false positive wastes one verification slot, a false negative loses one candidate. That is a far softer failure than the orchestrator implied when it called clock/power coupling urgent. THE ONE THING THAT STILL MATTERS: random lane noise merely costs efficiency, but SYSTEMATIC lane bias (e.g. lane 1 consistently hotter than lane 4) would systematically misrank candidates and therefore degrade the screen itself. The mitigation for that is already the right one and already identified: an A/A control across lanes, which detects systematic offset without needing any absolute accuracy. NET EFFECT ON DESIGN: this makes the partitioning argument STRONGER, not weaker. Because lanes need only preserve RANKING and never absolute accuracy, we can partition more aggressively than a claim-grade protocol would allow — the full-instance verification gate is what protects validity, and it is already in place.

steering_ledger.verbatim: you could make the metric richer by independently looking at the mtric across different model quantization (ex: MI210 works quite well at 16-bit but underperforms massively at 4-bit)
steering_ledger.effect: SHARPENS the roofline-utilisation target (seq 18 / AK-D35) from a scalar into a DIAGNOSTIC, and is also more correct than an aggregate. Two reasons. (1) CORRECTNESS: bytes-moved per weight is quant-dependent (Q4_K ~0.5 B/weight vs fp16 2 B/weight), so a single aggregate utilisation figure mixes different byte-movement regimes and is not a well-defined quantity. Per-quant is the only basis on which the denominator is meaningful. (2) DIAGNOSTIC POWER: a scalar says there is headroom; a per-quant curve says WHERE. If utilisation is high at bf16/fp16 and low at Q4_K/IQ2, the deficit is localised to the DEQUANT path rather than to the memory subsystem or general kernel quality — which is exactly the op class our kernel work targets (dequant GEMV named repeatedly across the Stage-2 dives, and mi210-q8-dequant-gemv-roofline.md owns it). Corroborating prior in our own record: iqk gives +33-43% prefill on K/legacy plus IQ2/IQ3/IQ4_XS while IQ1 remains stubbed, and the AVX512BW 8x8 Q8_0 work measured +31.8% at 1t — both are evidence that quant-path efficiency varies sharply and independently of the fp16 path. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE EXTERNAL ANCHOR: the SOTA-CUDA comparison must also be per-quant, or it compares our Q4 path against their fp16 path and manufactures a gap. AK-D35 already requires MoE be counted by active-expert bytes, which is the same principle applied to a different axis, so this extends an existing rule rather than adding one.
